title: Your elevator cable snaps 300 metres up. Jumping at the last second saves 4%

beats.say: Your elevator cable snaps 300 metres up. With no brakes, you hit the bottom at 276 kilometres an hour.
beats.speak: Your elevator cable snaps three hundred metres up. With no brakes, you hit the bottom at two hundred and seventy six kilometres an hour.

head: NOTHING
SLOWS IT DOWN.
beats.say: Nothing slows it down. Every second, it falls 9.81 metres per second faster. 300 metres takes just 7.82 seconds.
beats.speak: Nothing slows it down. Every second, it falls nine point eight one metres per second faster. Three hundred metres takes just seven point eight two seconds.

head: AND INSIDE,
YOU FLOAT.
beats.say: And inside, you float. You and the car fall at exactly the same rate, so the floor can't push on you.

head: JUMP AT THE
LAST SECOND?
beats.say: So jump at the last second? Your best jump pushes up at 3.13 metres per second. You still hit at 265 kilometres an hour. Just 4% slower.
beats.speak: So jump at the last second? Your best jump pushes up at three point one three metres per second. You still hit at two hundred and sixty five kilometres an hour. Just four percent slower.

head: NOW THE
BURJ KHALIFA.
beats.say: Now the Burj Khalifa. Its tallest service elevator travels 504 metres. Snap that cable and you fall for 10.14 seconds, and hit at 358 kilometres an hour.
beats.speak: Now the Burj Khalifa. Its tallest service elevator travels five hundred and four metres. Snap that cable and you fall for ten point one four seconds, and hit at three hundred and fifty eight kilometres an hour.

head: A NORMAL RIDE
THERE: 10 M/S.
beats.say: Its fastest passenger lifts ride at 10 metres per second. Free fall from the top would hit 9.94 times faster.
beats.speak: Its fastest passenger lifts ride at ten metres per second. Free fall from the top would hit nine point nine four times faster.

head: SOMEONE
LIVED THROUGH IT.
beats.say: In 1945, Betty Lou Oliver fell 75 floors, more than 300 metres, in an Empire State Building elevator. She survived. The snapped cable piled up like a spring, and air trapped in the shaft slowed the car.
beats.speak: In nineteen hundred and forty five, Betty Lou Oliver fell seventy five floors, more than three hundred metres, in an Empire State Building elevator. She survived. The snapped cable piled up like a spring, and air trapped in the shaft slowed the car.

head: WHY ELEVATORS
DON'T DROP.
beats.say: In 1854, Elisha Otis stood on a platform and had its rope cut in front of a crowd. His safety brake grabbed the rails. All safe, gentlemen, all safe.
beats.speak: In eighteen hundred and fifty four, Elisha Otis stood on a platform and had its rope cut in front of a crowd. His safety brake grabbed the rails. All safe, gentlemen, all safe.

beats.say: Follow Ship With Pip for more.

caption: What if your elevator cable snapped? From 300 m up, with no brakes and no air, the car falls for 7.82 seconds and hits at 276 km/h. Inside, you would float, because you and the car fall at the same rate. Jumping at the last second only takes off your jump speed, about 3.13 m/s: you still hit at 265 km/h, just 4% slower. From the top of the Burj Khalifa's tallest service elevator (504 m) you would fall for 10.14 seconds and hit at 358 km/h, 9.94 times faster than its 10 m/s passenger lifts. In 1945 Betty Lou Oliver survived a fall of 75 floors, more than 300 m, in an Empire State Building elevator: the snapped cables piled up like a spring and air pressure in the shaft slowed the car. And since 1854, when Elisha Otis had his own rope cut in front of a crowd, safety brakes grab the rails when a rope fails.
notes: Guinness World Records (Longest fall survived in a lift): Betty Lou Oliver, 28 July 1945, Empire State Building, survived a plunge of 75 stories (over 300 m or 1,000 ft); the impact was cushioned by the severed cables piling up in a spring-like spiral on the shaft floor, and the lift was slowed by air pressure in the relatively airtight shaft. We use 300 m, the lower bound Guinness gives, as the drop height. Burj Khalifa official fact sheet: tallest service elevator 504 m; observatory elevators travel at 10 m/s. Otis history page: Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety brake in 1854 at the Crystal Palace Exhibition in New York, standing on a raised platform while the rope was cut; he said 'All safe, gentlemen, all safe.' NIST: standard gravity 9.80665 m/s2 (shown as 9.81). The half metre jump (take-off speed 3.13 m/s) is the same chosen example as the jump reel. Physics: free fall with no drag and no brakes, v = sqrt(2gh), t = sqrt(2h/g); jumping subtracts your take-off speed from the car's speed. The animation is not real time.
